source.title: ZipIt! Merging Models from Different Tasks without Training
source.authors: George Stoica; Daniel Bolya; J. Bjorner; Pratik Ramesh; Taylor Hearn; Judy Hoffman

record.tranche_reason: The study measures cross-model activation correlations and finds they fall with depth, qualifying any claim of uniform convergence. It also shows that merging representations can preserve task performance only partly and that the outcome depends on where merging stops.
record.gate_note: The study reports average neuron correlations across layers and task performance after ZipIt! merges, including a different-output-modality setting. Its width-scaling results concern merged-model task accuracy, not direct representation similarity, so they do not test whether similarity itself rises with scale. Figure-only scaling results are not recorded as similarity rows.
record.test_reason: The study is mainly a merging method whose results are its own task accuracies (T4-like). One result bears on the claim: Appendix A, Table 5 reports average neuron-activation correlations between differently initialized ResNet-20 (8×) models trained on disjoint CIFAR-100 class halves. The correlations are moderate and fall with depth. This is a new setting (different seed plus disjoint label sets) with a direct, if thin, similarity result relevant to V3 and V7.
record.authors_conclusion: Mostly correct. The authors conclude that ZipIt!, by merging features within and across models and by partial zipping, greatly outperforms permutation-based merging on disjoint-task models without retraining. In Appendix A they report that cross-model correlations consistently decrease with depth, consistent with later layers encoding task-specific features, and that this tracks the drop in merged performance.
record.recipe_differences: ZipIt! uses activation-correlation-based feature matching, permits within-model feature merges, and supports partial zipping; the study does not use a direct distance-similarity convergence test.
record.method_sensitivity: Layer/depth and the stopping point for partial zipping change activation correlations and task performance.

fits_no_version.finding: Merged-model task accuracy relative to the ensemble falls the more layers are merged, across CIFAR, ImageNet, multi-dataset and segmentation+classification settings (Tables 1–3, 9). The authors link this to declining layer similarity (Table 5 with Fig. 7a).
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: Weight-space mergeability of independently trained models on disjoint tasks declines with depth, tracking declining activation correlation.

fits_no_version.finding: As ResNet-20 width grows, ZipIt! merged accuracy approaches the ensemble while permutation baselines plateau near 45% (Fig. 6b, Table 8). The authors credit extra within-model redundancy, not cross-model convergence.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: Wider models contain more within-model redundant features that make cross-task merging easier.

record.problems: The correlation results are averages for the model set, not per-pair results. The different-modality table does not report uncertainty, and task performance after merging is an indirect measure of representation interchangeability rather than a direct comparison of induced distances.
record.rows_left_out: Other task-accuracy comparisons for CIFAR, ImageNet, multi-dataset classification, and ablations (Sections 5–6 and Appendices D, E, and H) are not extracted here; they report downstream merging performance rather than direct representation-similarity measurements. The width sweep in Figure 6 reports merged-model accuracy, not representation similarity.

untested.parts: Representation similarity is not measured as a function of scale. Fig. 6b and Table 8 report merged-model accuracy against width, not alignment.
Entirely untested: no vision-language or paired image-caption data.
Same-data, different-seed pairs are not measured for correlation. Feature identity, shared subspaces, and unit- versus basis-level differences are not analysed.
No linear map, stitching, relative representations or unpaired mapping between representations is evaluated as such.
No interpretable features, neurons or circuits are compared across models.
Only one similarity measure (activation correlation) is used. Neighbour settings and out-of-distribution inputs are not varied. Data amount is ablated only for merging accuracy (Fig. 8).
No test of whether shared data or objectives, rather than a common model of reality, explain the alignment; no plateau analysis of similarity.

record.verdict_notes: The only similarity measurement is Table 5 (three averages, one model set, no baseline). Its bearing on V3 is confounded because the paired models differ in training classes as well as initialization. Rows r4–r7 are the study's own method performance and should not carry versions. Relation could arguably be T4 apart from Table 5.

versions.untested_parts: The width sweep reports merged-model accuracy, not whether representation distances or alignment rise with model scale and capability.
No vision-language model comparison or paired image-caption representation alignment.

The study measures average activation correlations for same-architecture models trained on disjoint class splits, not feature identities, shared subspaces, or whether individual units and bases differ.
The study tests ZipIt! feature merging and task performance, not a standalone linear representation map, stitching layers, relative representations, or mapping without paired data.
No interpretable features, neurons, SAE features, or circuits are identified across models.
The study varies layer/depth and reports correlations, but does not compare alternative similarity measures, neighbour settings, or out-of-distribution inputs.
The study shows incomplete and depth-dependent alignment, but does not establish whether shared training data or objectives, rather than a common model of reality, explain it.

relationships.condition: Differently initialized ResNet-20 (8×) pairs trained on disjoint CIFAR-100 50+50 class splits
relationships.reason: Average cross-model activation correlation is only moderate and declines with depth (0.50, 0.37, 0.27 at layers 7, 13, 19 of 20). Shared features are thus concentrated in early layers when training classes differ (r1–r3).
relationships.display_finding: Average cross-model activation correlation declined from 0.50 to 0.37 to 0.27 at layers 7, 13, and 19 of 20, respectively.

source_check.reason: Rows r1–r3 show incomplete activation correspondence that declines with depth in this disjoint-task setting. Task and initialization differences are confounded, so this qualifies convergence under task differences without isolating seed effects.

relationships.condition: Differently initialized ResNet-20 (8×) pairs trained on disjoint CIFAR-100 class splits
relationships.reason: Cross-model correlations stay far from complete (at most 0.50) and fall to 0.27 in late layers. The authors attribute this to task-specific features, which fits the incompleteness part of V7 (r1–r3).
relationships.display_finding: Cross-model correlations reached at most 0.50 and fell to 0.27 in late layers, which the authors attributed to task-specific features.
